data.content:
Rosetta Stone
A granodiorite stele bearing a decree issued at Memphis in 196 BC on behalf of King Ptolemy V of Egypt, containing text preserved in three scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Egyptian Demotic, and Ancient Greek. It is incomplete but serves as the key that allowed scholars to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.

Memphis Decree
The decree issued at Memphis in 196 BC on behalf of King Ptolemy V of Egypt, affirming the royal cult of Ptolemy V and listing benefits granted to temples by a council of Egyptian priests.

King Ptolemy V
The pharaoh who ruled Egypt in 196 BC upon whose coronation the Memphis Decree was issued one year after his reign began.

French soldiers
Troops led by Napoleon Bonaparte during their military campaign in Egypt where they discovered the Rosetta Stone in 1799.<SEP>Troops during Napoleon Bonaparte's campaign who discovered the Rosetta Stone near el-Rashid in 1799.

Napoleon Bonaparte
The French general whose military campaign in Egypt resulted in the discovery of the Rosetta Stone.

el-Rashid
The town where the Rosetta Stone was found near the Nile Delta while troops were carrying out demolition and construction work on a fort.

Pierre-François Bouchard
An engineer serving with the French expedition who is generally credited with recognizing the significance of the Rosetta Stone.

British Museum
The institution that has held the Rosetta Stone in London since 1802, where it remains one of the most visited objects.

London
The city in England where the Rosetta Stone has been housed by the British Museum since 1802.

Thomas Young
An English polymath who made early progress in deciphering hieroglyphs in the 1810s by correctly identifying that some signs recorded royal names.

Jean-François Champollion
A French scholar who announced in 1822 that he had cracked the hieroglyphic writing system, building on Thomas Young's work and his own analysis of the cartouche of Ptolemy V.

Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres
The Parisian academy where Jean-François Champollion read a letter announcing his breakthrough in deciphering hieroglyphs in September 1822.

Akhenaten
The pharaoh known for promoting the worship of the sun disk Aten, who was the father of Tutankhamun.

Tutankhamun
A member of the 18th Dynasty who became pharaoh around 1332 BCE, ruled for roughly ten years, and died young with his tomb escaping large-scale looting.

Howard Carter
A British archaeologist who led the excavation of Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings starting in 1922.

Lord Carnarvon
The patron named George Herbert, 5th Earl of Carnarvon, whose full name is recorded, who funded Howard Carter's excavation and died shortly after the tomb was opened.

KV62
The designation for Tutankhamun's tomb located in the Valley of the Kings, discovered on November 4, 1922.

George Herbert
The full name of Lord Carnarvon (5th Earl of Carnarvon), who served as Howard Carter's patron for the excavation of Tutankhamun's tomb.

Georgi Herbert
The location of the Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza pyramids where many artifacts from Tutankhamun's tomb, including the gold mask, were later moved after being initially housed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

Egyptian Museum
The institution in Cairo that initially housed artifacts from Tutankhamun's tomb before many were moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza pyramids.

Hieroglyphs
The writing system preserved on the Rosetta Stone which was unreadable for centuries until scholars could decipher it using the stone's text.

Great Wall of China
A UNESCO World Heritage Site designated in 1987, recognized as a powerful symbol of Chinese engineering and endurance, having largely lost its military significance after the fall of the Ming Dynasty.<SEP>The series of fortifications across northern China, largely rebuilt by the Ming Dynasty using fired brick and cut stone, featuring watchtowers and integrated natural defenses like rivers and ridges.<SEP>A defensive structure stretching approximately 8,850 kilometers, featuring over 25,000 watchtowers and serving as a symbol of Chinese engineering.

Warring States period
An era in ancient Chinese history dating back over two thousand years, characterized by territorial competition among states leading up to unification under Qin Shi Huang.

Emperor Qin Shi Huang
The ruler who unified China in 221 BCE and initiated early wall-building efforts along the northern frontier using rammed earth.

Ming Dynasty
A Chinese imperial dynasty that fell in 1644 after the strategic pass at Shanhaiguan was opened by its general Wu Sangui.<SEP>The Chinese dynasty that ruled from 1368 to 1644, responsible for the most visible and well-preserved sections of the Great Wall.

Zhu Yuanzhang
Also known as the Hongwu Emperor; founder of the Ming Dynasty who initiated major wall-building efforts as a defense against Mongol tribes.

Beijing
The capital city located near strategically important sections of the Great Wall where fired brick and cut stone were heavily used.

data.entity_name: China's State Administration of Cultural Heritage
data.content:
China's State Administration of Cultural Heritage
The government body that conducted a 2009 survey using infrared and GPS mapping technology to measure the full extent of the Ming wall.

Badaling
A well-fortified section of the Great Wall located about 70 kilometers northwest of Beijing, opened to tourists in 1957 and extensively restored.

Mutianyu
Another well-known Ming-era section of the Great Wall first built in 1368 under general Xu Da.

Nine Frontier Garrisons
A defensive organizational system comprising nine defense zones with regional military governors, integrated into the broader wall network.

Manchu forces
The military group that entered through the Shanhaiguan pass in 1644, establishing the Qing Dynasty after suppressing Li Zicheng's rebellion.

Qing Dynasty
A Chinese dynasty established in 1644 when Manchu forces entered China through the pass at Shanhaiguan, enabled by Wu Sangui's strategic decision to suppress Li Zicheng's rebellion.<SEP>The dynasty established by Manchu forces in 1644 following their entry into Beijing through the Great Wall's strategic pass at Shanhaiguan.<SEP>The dynasty established after Manchu forces entered through Shanhaiguan to suppress Li Zicheng's rebellion.

Li Zicheng
The leader of a rebellion whose suppression required assistance from the Ming forces, including those led by Wu Sangui.<SEP>A rebel leader whose suppression helped suppress a rebellion, leading to the opening of the Shanhaiguan pass by Wu Sangui.

Wu Sangui
The Ming general who opened the strategic pass at Shanhaiguan, allowing Manchu forces through to help suppress the rebellion led by Li Zicheng, an act that inadvertently enabled the Manchus to establish the Qing Dynasty.<SEP>A Ming general who opened the strategic pass at Shanhaiguan in 1644 to help suppress Li Zicheng's rebellion, inadvertently enabling Manchu forces.

Ming construction
The building efforts that intensified after Mongol raids in the 15th century and continued for roughly two hundred years under the Ming Dynasty.

infrared and GPS mapping technology
Techniques used by China's State Administration of Cultural Heritage in 2009 to measure the full extent of the Great Wall.

visual signaling
A method using smoke by day and fire by night to warn of approaching threats from watchtowers spaced along the wall.

Garrisons
Military units stationed at forts along the length of the Great Wall.

Shanhaiguan
The strategic pass of the Great Wall where General Wu Sangui opened it in 1644 to allow Manchu forces through.<SEP>A strategic pass on the Great Wall where Manchu forces entered in 1644.

military significance
The role and importance of the Great Wall as a defensive barrier, which largely ended after 1644.

Orville Wright
One of the brothers who achieved the first powered flight on December 17, 1903; he piloted the first flight of the day and later founded the Wright Company.

Wilbur Wright
One of the brothers who achieved the first powered flight on December 17, 1903; he piloted the longest flight of that morning and died of typhoid fever in 1912.

Wright Flyer
The aircraft used for the first sustained, controlled flight of a powered, heavier-than-air aircraft on December 17, 1903.

Kitty Hawk
The site near North Carolina where the Wright brothers achieved their first powered flight; specifically the sandy dunes called Kill Devil Hills.

Orville and Wilbur Wright
A team of brothers who ran a bicycle repair shop in Dayton, Ohio, and studied aerodynamics before achieving flight.

Charlie Taylor
The mechanic who helped the Wright brothers design the engine for their aircraft.

Dayton
The city in Ohio where the Wright brothers ran their bicycle repair shop and wind tunnel laboratory.

Twelve-horsepower gasoline engine
A custom-built engine that powered the Wright Flyer, designed with help from Charlie Taylor.

John T. Daniels
A local businessman and photographer who captured the famous photograph of the first flight before operating a camera.

Kill Devil Hills
The specific site within Kitty Hawk where the Wright brothers conducted testing and flew in 1903.

Wright Company
A company founded by Orville and Wilbur Wright in 1909 to manufacture aircraft commercially.

data.entity_name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
data.content:
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
The institution in Washington, D.C. where the original 1903 Wright Flyer is currently preserved.

Great Wall
A historic fortification that served as a strategic barrier against invasions but ultimately failed to prevent the fall of the Ming Dynasty.

Manchus
A group of people who established the Qing Dynasty in 1644 after entering China through the opened pass at Shanhaiguan due to Wu Sangui's actions.
